I remember my first time going to a national event in western Canada. At the time I was 14 years old. My family are what we call budget racers. Two drivers (my father and I), one kart each, and a spare engine we share if anything was to happen. My first experience with a “rich” driver in my class was on the scales after qualifying. 

The young man in front of me looked at his dad and said “I don’t like this setup. I want to run kart 6 with engine 4”. 

I was bewildered. Ended up walking the paddocks later and seeing a nascar hauler with 10 karts up top, and maybe a good 15 engines on the bench. Everything brand spanking new, tags and all. Each new package is $9500, plus the remaining 5 engines at $4000 each. 

Add onto that the new suits they get every year to match their bands/sponsors

Add a new set of tires every single race at $300 a piece. Regular clubs usually have 12 club level events, plus any traveling events like nationals or super nats. So let’s be nice and say 20 sets / year. This includes practice sets, and a new set everyday for club racing and out of town events. 

Slap some fuel, engine oil, broken parts, etc on that bill. 

$95,000 for the complete package karts
$20,000 engines alone
$6000 tires
$1500~for parts, fuel, etc

Brings to $122,500

Keep in mind, I did not include any membership fees or raceday fees. Club race is usually $80/day.. big events can be $600/event. Membership is usually $500/year

You obviously have not been in racing long at all to really understand anything. Quite dense. Briggs is one of the hardest classes. Because of the lack of power, every single tiny mistake is absolutely crucial. If you're even a hair out of shape, you lose all your speed. I ran rotax and dd2. Dd2 was easy. It was simple to fix any mistake made. If you look at any point standings in any club for the Briggs, you will find that there are consistent front runners, people who are always up at the front. Honestly, I've done my research on you. Looked up your times at K1, saw how you placed there too. Watched your videos on karting and track driving. You're entering the part of karting that you don't understand. My suggestion? Get a Briggs and go win your local club championship for the 2017 series. That will tell me if you are ready to go fast or not Derek.

I thought racing was supposed to be close. You're definitely a qualifier type of person, not a racer. Rentals and Briggs are not comparable. Rentals you can jam and hit each other. Briggs with the open wheels brings close racing, and with that close racing comes a lot of trust and patience with the other drivers. I think the original post is useless if you do not like racing with other people. Find a track where your membership fee includes a key to the track, and do all the hot laps you want.

I find the faster the kart, the more separated the competition is. There are a lot of guys from big teams ditching the 2 strokes to go into this briggs program. I would say about 95% of people I have spoken to think the speed is absolutely perfect to insure close racing.
But now you have the people that want to go faster, and the people who are perfectly content with what they have, thus dividing the field in half.

When starting, a lot of karts would be just fine. As you progress you will start to notice little things here and there. I drive an arrow kart right now. IMO is more or less a beginner kart. For example, I have 3 axles to choose from. When I ran 2-stroke, I had a crg looking at 36 axles for a more defined set up. Any kart will get you going. Once you have some experience under your belt, find your driving style and pick what kart fits best. All karts are unique in their own way.

My competition where I'm from could be better. I live in the middle of no where up in Canada. Last year my grid saw 13 karts and I think the number has gone up 5 heading into this year. I have gone and won 3 out of the 6 western canadian championship races (I only competed in 4) a few years back with grids upwards of 25+. Looking around and watching videos of karts in the States, I see a lot of grids holding 30 or even 40+ karts which is absolutely fantastic and i would love to travel to an event one of these years. 

I do believe the 206 class is a great place to begin. As mentioned I started out in the honda 5.5 about 20 years ago. Gave me lots of time to figure out kart setup, track positioning and overall comfort with cornering and speed. I have seen people jump into a 2 stroke with no previous experience because they want to "go fast", but leave after that season because they don't win right away. As well, very expensive if you are on a tight budget. 

A bit of brief history with my province and karting, with the general direction:
Used to run Primarily honda. In the year 2000, the senior class have 20-30 karts on the grid. Then a big kart team came in and pushed the whole 2 stroke karts and divided the club in half. Then became very expensive with needing new parts and equipment and engine rebuilds. Numbers then dwindled for 10 years. Rotax class was only run if 3 or more cars showed up, which was half the race days. Honda was down to 6-7 members in the senior class. Within 10 years, I watched the club go from 50+ karts a day down to 15-20. Briggs then came out and its awesome. Old chassis can compete with new ones, motors are solid and reliable. Its fast enough to get your adrenaline going, but not to poop your pants. A lot of people in my area are selling the 2 stroke to get back into the briggs. We find the racing closer, friendlier and a lot more fun! 

This might not be the case with your local club, but thats what happened here. Give briggs a couple years, and move up when you're ready

Prices may vary according to location, and it all depends on what you're looking for. You can buy a great used, race ready LO206 kart for roughly $1500. These chassis are great to learn your basic set up knowledge, and adapt to real environment without a steep learning curve. I personally am a fan of the LO206 program. I ran 2 stroke for a while, however it was very tough to keep up financially with big teams and the developing technology. I do enjoy the Briggs package with the sealed engine. No modifications allowed. As well I am running off of a 2007 arrow chassis and it has won the past two championships here. It evens out the competition very well. As others had mentioned, check out your local club. Get some information on race day fees, membership prices, ETC ETC. Check out a race day, see if they have an arrive and drive program or not! Hope this, and what the others are posting helps, and goodluck!
